Hyperphosphatasia with mental retardation syndrome is a heterogeneous genetic condition.

Two siblings aged 5 years and 3 years were evaluated for global development delay and facial dysmorphism. A novel missense variant, c.851A>G (p. H284R, NM_033419.3), in PGAP3 was identiﬁed using wholeexome sequencing. Assays for elevated alkaline phosphatase and exome sequencing can be useful for the diagnosis of hyperphosphatasia with mental retardation syndrome.

Abstract Keywords ► hyperphosphatasia with mental retardation syndrome ► PGAP3 ► exome sequencing ► alkaline phosphatase Introduction Six subtypes of hyperphosphatasia with mental retardation syndrome or Mabry syndrome (HPMRS; MIM 239300) are reported based on their molecular basis and are caused by the genes including PIGV, PIGY, PIGO, PGAP2, PIGW, and PGAP3.1–4 Clinically, it shows variable expressivity ranging from severe syndromic forms to isolated mild intellectual disability. Ten additional pathogenic variants in PGAP3 causing Mabry syndrome are reported till date.

We report an Omani consanguineous family with two siblings bearing a novel missense variant, c.851A>G (p. H284R, NM_033419.3), and delineate additional features of this condition. Materials and Methods Patients Two siblings, born to thirddegree consanguineous parents from Oman, were brought for evaluation of global develop- ment delay and lack of speech (►Fig. 1A). The elder child (IV1) was a 5year-old boy.

Respiratory distress and feeding difﬁculty were noted soon after birth (birth weight: 3.2 kg, normal) for which he required mechanical ventilation for 10 days. He was on nasogastric feeding up to 2 months of age. He had not attained any gross motor milestones or speech by 5 years of age.
He is presently wheelchair bound. He had febrile seizures at 3 years of age. Cleft palate was noted at birth for which he underwent cleft palate repair at 1 year of age.

He also had myringotomy with grommet insertion at 2 years. On examination, he was 107 cm tall (3–50th centile), weighed 16 kg (3–50th centile), and had an occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) of 50 cm (3–50th centile). Facial dysmorphic features included deep set eyes, narrow and upslanting palpebral ﬁssures, ptosis, low set large ﬂeshy ear lobes, broad nasal root with a squared nasal tip, long smooth philtrum, exaggerated cupid’s bow, thin vermilion of upper lip, and posterior cleft palate.

Serum alkaline phosphatase was elevated (644 IU/L; normal range: 10–80 IU/L). Echocardiography showed atrial and ventricular septal defects. Fundus evaluation showed bilateral large discs with tilting of left optic disc.

Brainstem auditory evoked response showed severe sensory neural hearing loss. His younger sister (IV2) was 3 years old who had a similar postnatal history with a weak cry at birth and required immediate intubation and ventilation. She had a birth weight of 3.5 kg (normal).

She, too, had posterior cleft palate and severe retrognathia for which she underwent cleft palate repair and distraction osteogenesis at 2 months. The cleft palate was repaired at 1 year. At 3 years, she was noted to have global development delay with no speech.

She had behavioral problems in the form of selfbiting. She was 93 cm tall (3–50th centile), weighed 10 kg (<3rd centile), and had an OFC of 46.5 cm (at 3rd centile). She had microcephaly, upslanting narrow palpebral ﬁssures, epicanthic folds, broad nasal root with squared nasal tip, low set large ﬂeshy earlobes, long smooth philtrum and exaggerated cupid’s bow, sagging cheeks and lower jaw, and microdontia (►Fig. 1C).
Serum alkaline phosphatase was elevated (613 IU/L). Echocardiography returned normal ﬁndings. Fundus evaluation showed thin temporal crescents.

Discussion Both the siblings had distinct facial dysmorphism similar to the previously reported individuals with Mabry syndrome.5,6 Ptosis and optic disc changes were novel phenotypic features observed in our patients. The consistent dysmorphic features of this condition include upslanting narrow palpebral ﬁssures, broad nasal bridge, large ﬂeshy ear lobes, long smooth philtrum, thin vermilion of upper lip, sagging cheeks, small chin, and cleft palate, along with intellectual disability, behavioral problems, seizures, and lack of speech.

PGAP3 encodes a glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI)-specific phospholipase A2 expressed in the Golgi complex. Function of the enzyme is important for fatty acid remodeling.6 About 27 genes involved in the functioning of GPI anchored proteins have been described. Missense variants are the most common mutations reported till date, supporting the assumption that GPI anchor deﬁciencies have residual activity of GPIanchored proteins.

It has been observed that all the missense variants in PGAP3 show a reduced activity of PGAP3 protein, one of which was observed in the same exon and protein domain. Other truncating frameshift and nonsense variants are reported in compound heterozygous state in association with a missense mutation.5,6 This probably makes the condition nonlethal despite being a major hindrance in embryogenesis.

Hyperphosphatasia with Mental Retardation Syndrome Nampoothiri et al. 193 As a preliminary step, serum alkaline phosphatase may be offered to all children with intellectual disability and facial dysmorphism and can be quite handy in diagnosing this group of disorders. The absence of congenital cataract, elevated serum creatinine kinase, and renal involvement distinguishe the condition from the PIGY type, reported by two families.7 PIGW has been implicated in this condition in just one family.1 Combining the typical phenotype with the elevated alkaline phosphatase level will help to narrow down the molecular analysis to a panel of four genes, PIGV, PIGO, PGAP2, and PGAP3.

Lack of brachytelephalangy further helps to point toward PGAP3 rather than allelic variants due to PIGV, PIGO, and PGAP2. In conclusion, global developmental delay and facial dysmorphism in the presence of elevated alkaline phosphatase is an important clue for HPMRS. This work also highlights the successful application of exome sequencing in genetically heterogeneous conditions often encountered in pediatric practice.
